messages.content: Why does the picture made by a lens come out upside down on a wall? I thought the lens simply shrank the view and laid it on the wall, so turning it over seems like an extra thing the glass somehow does.

The lens does not flip a finished picture. Light from each point spreads out, and the lens bends those rays so they meet again. Rays from the top of the object cross the central region and meet near the bottom of the image; rays from the bottom meet near the top. That crossing creates the inversion naturally.
What makes those lines of light cross instead of just getting squeezed closer together? Is there one crossing place for the whole object, or does every little part have its own meeting spot?

Every small object point has its own matching image point. The curved surfaces change a ray's direction by different amounts depending on where it enters. For one object point, those differently bent rays converge at one location. The collection of many such locations forms the picture, so there is no single crossing point shared by the entire object.
If I slide the object closer, I assume the glass gets a shorter focal length because the crossing moves. Is focal length just the distance from the lens to wherever the sharp picture happens to land?

For a fixed lens in the same surrounding material, its focal length stays essentially fixed. What changes is the image distance. Focal length is defined using incoming rays that are parallel, as from a very distant object. For nearer objects, the rays arrive already spreading, so the lens needs more distance after bending them before they meet.
Then why does the image disappear from the wall when the object gets very close? The light is still crossing somewhere, so I would expect moving the wall far enough back to find it again.

Once the object is closer than one focal length, the rays leave the lens still spreading rather than converging. Your eyes can trace them backward to an apparent point, producing an upright virtual image, but no wall can catch that apparent meeting. Moving the wall cannot help because the rays never physically reunite on that side.

What decides how much larger a lens makes something look? It seems obvious that a wider piece of glass must give more magnification, because it has more bending area and can spread the picture across more space.

Width mainly controls how much light the lens collects, not how large the image is. Magnification is set by the object's position, the image's position, and the lens's focal length. A wider lens of the same shape and material usually gives the same image size, but it can make that image brighter by admitting more rays.
Why does moving the object matter if the lens bends every ray by the same amount? I can see how the picture would move forward or backward, but not why its height should change too.

The lens does not turn every ray through one fixed angle. Its effect depends on the ray's incoming direction and where it crosses the curved surface. When the object moves, the bundle reaching the lens has a different spread. The new geometry changes both where corresponding rays meet and the height of those meeting points.
Suppose I keep the object still and replace the lens with a bigger circle cut from the same kind of curve. Would the picture stay exactly the same size while only becoming brighter?

Ideally, yes: if the curvature, material, and thickness pattern are unchanged, enlarging the clear opening does not change focal length or magnification. It admits additional outer rays, increasing brightness. Real lenses can show more blur near their edges, so opening the full diameter may also reveal aberrations that a smaller opening hides.
Is that why a small hole can make a picture look sharper even though it looks dimmer? I had assumed sharpness and magnification were basically the same improvement, just described in different ways.

They are separate properties. Magnification describes image size relative to object size. Sharpness describes how tightly light from one object point is confined in the image. A smaller opening blocks troublesome outer rays and increases depth of field, often improving apparent sharpness, but it does not provide extra magnification and eventually diffraction adds blur.
Then what everyday change would actually increase the magnification without swapping the lens? Do I move the object toward the focus mark and chase the sharp image with the wall?

For a converging lens making a real image, move the object closer to the focal point while keeping it just outside that distance, then move the wall farther away to regain focus. The resulting image grows. This changes the object and image distances, while the lens's own focal length remains unchanged.

Why can a magnifying glass show an upright enlarged word when a lens projecting onto paper makes an upside-down picture? I thought enlargement came from using a larger lens, so the different direction is confusing.

The difference comes from where the object sits relative to the focal length, not from the lens diameter. Outside one focal length, outgoing rays can meet and form an inverted real image. Inside one focal length, they remain spread out; your eye traces them backward and sees an upright, enlarged virtual image on the object's side.
What does tracing backward mean here? The letters seem to be sitting behind the glass, and I am actually seeing them, so calling their location only apparent sounds like the light is somehow false.

The light is completely real; only its apparent source is different from its physical path. Your visual system usually assumes rays reaching the eye traveled in straight lines. After the lens bends spreading rays toward your eye, extending their final paths backward makes them seem to originate from a larger, more distant word.
Could I put a sheet where that larger word seems to be and get the same view printed on it? If not, what exactly prevents the sheet from catching the apparent picture?

No. At that apparent location, the outgoing rays are not actually passing through the corresponding image points; only backward extensions of their paths intersect there. A sheet records light that physically arrives at each spot. Since the rays are diverging, no placement on that side assembles them into the enlarged pattern your eye infers.
So if I move the word just beyond the special focus distance, what should I notice first: the upright view turning over, the image becoming smaller, or the place where it looks located changing?

Near the focal point, the apparent image moves extremely far away and the emerging rays approach parallel. Just beyond the focal distance, a real inverted image forms very far on the other side. As you move the word farther from the lens, that real image comes closer and generally becomes smaller. The transition is not a simple flip at one visible plane.

If a lens makes a blurry patch on a wall, why does sliding the wall sometimes make a detailed picture appear? I am fairly sure moving the wall changes the lens's focal length by giving the light a new stopping place.

Sliding the wall does not alter the lens's focal length. For a fixed object position, the lens sends rays from each object point toward a particular image plane. At that plane they form tight spots; before or after it, each bundle is still converging or has begun spreading, so neighboring spots overlap and look blurry.
What is the wall doing at the sharp position besides stopping the rays? Does the picture already exist in the air there, or does the paper somehow organize the light when it arrives?

The ray pattern exists at that plane before the wall is added. The wall mainly scatters the arriving light in many directions so your eyes can view it. It does not organize the image. Dust or mist can reveal parts of beams in the air, but placing a screen at the image plane makes the full pattern easy to see.
Why is there only one good wall position for one object distance? A thick object has a front and back, so I would think different parts demand different wall positions at the same time.

That is correct for a three-dimensional object. Points at different distances have slightly different best image distances. A single flat screen can coincide perfectly with only one of those planes, though nearby planes may look acceptably sharp. The range that appears sharp is called depth of field, and a smaller lens opening usually enlarges it.
If I move the object farther away while leaving the wall fixed, which way should I move the lens to recover the picture? I keep guessing the same direction as the object, but I cannot picture why.

As an object moves farther from a converging lens, its sharp real image moves closer to the lens, approaching one focal length away. With the wall fixed, you therefore move the lens so the required image distance matches the lens-to-wall gap. The exact direction in the room depends on which item you hold fixed, so distances are safer than a memorized direction.
What happens if the wall is tilted rather than straight across from the lens? Would one edge focus because it is closer while the other edge stays smeared, or can the lens tilt the picture too?

With the object and lens kept parallel, a tilted wall cuts through the image plane at an angle, so typically only a strip is sharply focused. Tilting the lens changes the geometry and can tilt the plane of sharp focus, a principle used in view cameras. It also introduces distortions, so alignment matters as well as distance.
Would making the glass wider solve that tilted-wall blur by covering more possible meeting places? My picture is that a bigger lens creates a larger focus zone, even if the distances stay unchanged.

A wider opening usually does the opposite: it makes defocus more noticeable because rays arrive over a broader range of angles. It gathers more light but narrows the range of positions that look acceptably sharp. Reducing the opening can hide some tilted-screen blur, though it cannot make a genuinely tilted plane coincide with a parallel image plane.

What happens to all the different light lines leaving one point when they enter a lens? I picture the glass giving every line the same inward turn, with the lens size deciding how enlarged the final picture becomes.

A lens changes each ray according to the angle at which it meets each surface. Rays entering near different parts therefore receive different direction changes, arranged so they converge approximately at one image point. The lens diameter decides how many of those rays are accepted; image magnification comes from the object and image geometry instead.
Why do ray drawings usually show only three neat lines, then? If light leaves the point in every direction, those few lines seem too special to explain the whole bright patch.

Those are convenient construction rays, not the only rays present. One parallel to the axis refracts through the far focal point, one through the optical center is approximately undeviated, and one aimed through the near focal point emerges parallel. Their intersection locates the image point; all other admitted rays should converge there too in an ideal lens.
Is the line through the middle truly unbent, or is that another drawing shortcut? The glass still has two surfaces there, so it seems odd that this particular light line gets a free pass.

It is a thin-lens approximation. Near the optical center, the two surfaces are locally close to parallel, so the ray bends at both boundaries but emerges nearly parallel to its original direction, with only a small sideways shift. Thick lenses require more careful reference planes, and an off-axis central ray may not behave so simply.
Then why does blocking most of the lens not remove most of the picture? I would expect each patch of glass to carry one matching patch of the object, like pieces of a window view.

Every small region of the lens receives rays from nearly every visible object point. Blocking part of the lens removes some rays from every image point, so the whole picture remains but becomes dimmer. It may also become sharper by losing aberrant outer rays. A patch maps ray direction, not a matching tile of the finished image.
What is special about the focus mark of a lens? I have been treating it as the place where any object makes a sharp picture, and I assume it shifts closer to the glass when I move the object closer.

The focal point is where rays arriving parallel to the axis meet after a converging lens. Those rays correspond approximately to an object extremely far away. A nearby object sends spreading rays, so its image forms beyond the focal point. Moving that object changes the image location, while the focal length of the unchanged lens stays fixed.
Why do the rays come out parallel when the object itself sits on the focus mark? They started by spreading from one spot, so I do not see how parallel lines can still contain a picture.

For one object point on the focal plane, the lens converts its spreading bundle into a parallel bundle traveling in a particular direction. Different points across the object produce parallel bundles with different directions. The image information is therefore carried in angle rather than gathered into a finite image plane; another lens can convert those directions back into positions.
Could an extremely distant wall catch that picture, since parallel lines must eventually reach it? Or does the picture count as being infinitely far away even though every ray hits some real surface?

A distant wall receives the rays, but each parallel bundle stays broad instead of converging to one corresponding point. Bundles from different object points overlap, so the wall does not show a focused picture. Saying the image is at infinity is shorthand for the outgoing bundles being parallel and requiring infinite distance to converge under the simple geometric model.
If I place a second lens in those parallel lines, what decides where the picture returns? I would guess the first lens's new focal length still controls the landing place after I moved the object.

The first lens has not acquired a new focal length. It prepares bundles whose directions encode object position. The second lens brings each parallel bundle to a point in its own focal plane, so that second focal length largely sets the final image scale and location. This is the basic geometry behind telescopes and some relay systems.

Does that mean sliding the second lens along a perfectly parallel bundle should not change where the picture sits relative to that lens? That sounds different from focusing a single lens on a nearby object.

Yes, in the ideal parallel region, sliding the second lens leaves the final image one focal length behind that lens, so the image moves along with it. A nearby object does not supply parallel bundles, and changing the lens position then changes both object distance and required image distance. Real beams have finite width and alignment limits.

Why does a lens that caves inward make things look smaller instead of forming a little picture on the other side? I thought choosing a sufficiently large piece would eventually give enough magnification to project it.

An inward-curving, or diverging, lens spreads parallel rays rather than bringing them together. Its diameter can collect more rays, but it does not reverse that spreading action. For a normal real object by itself, the outgoing rays appear to come from a smaller upright virtual image on the object's side, so no screen on the far side catches it.
What is a negative focus supposed to mean? A distance cannot really be less than nothing, so I imagine it is just a label for a weak lens rather than an actual place.

The negative sign records direction, not a physically negative length. After a diverging lens, parallel rays spread as though they originated from a point on the incoming side. Extending the outgoing rays backward locates that focal point. Under the usual sign convention, its side makes the focal length negative; strength is described by the magnitude.
Can that spreading lens ever help make a real picture, or is it only useful for shrinking what the eye sees? I have seen paired lenses but cannot tell which one does the actual picture-making.

It can help within a combination. A converging lens may first create a bundle that is already heading toward a meeting point; a diverging lens can weaken that convergence, moving the final image farther away or changing its size. In a multi-lens system, image formation belongs to the sequence, not exclusively to one piece.
If I hold the two lenses together, do their powers simply cancel when their curves look equally strong? The thicknesses look similar, so I would expect no bending and no image change.

They cancel only if their optical powers are equal and opposite. Power depends on surface curvatures, refractive index, thickness, and surrounding material, so appearance alone is unreliable. For thin lenses touching each other, powers approximately add. A zero sum makes the pair afocal, but rays can still shift or show imperfections in real elements.

If a wider lens gathers more light, why does opening a camera lens make the background blurrier? Bigger glass should make everything larger and therefore easier to see clearly, since magnification only comes from lens size.

Opening the aperture uses a wider portion of the lens, but it does not by itself enlarge the image. It admits rays over a broader range of angles. At the exact image plane those rays meet, while slightly nearer or farther planes produce larger blur circles. Consequently, a wide opening gives more light but less depth of field.
What is a blur circle in ordinary terms? I picture an unfocused point turning into a fuzzy dot, but I do not know why the dot's width follows the opening rather than the glass curve.

Imagine a cone of rays narrowing toward its correct image point and widening after it. A sensor placed away from the cone's tip cuts it as a small disk rather than a point. A wider aperture makes the cone broader and steeper, so the same focusing error produces a larger disk. Curvature still determines where the tip belongs.
Why can the main subject stay the same size when the opening changes? If extra edge rays join the picture, I would expect them to extend its borders instead of piling onto the same points.

Edge rays from a given object point are directed toward the same corresponding image point as central rays. They add brightness at that point rather than creating more distant image points. The picture's borders come from which object points are included and the system's magnification, while the aperture controls how many paths from each point get through.
Does closing the opening always keep adding sharpness, then? A tiny gap seems as if it should select one perfect line from every point and remove nearly all the ways light can miss.

Only up to a point. Closing the aperture reduces defocus and many lens aberrations, but a very small opening makes light spread by diffraction. The image then softens even at perfect focus. Practical systems balance aberration, diffraction, brightness, and desired depth of field rather than treating the smallest opening as automatically best.
If the object moves closer while the opening stays fixed, does the focal length shorten to keep the cone tip near the sensor? Cameras seem to adjust something without moving very far.

Ordinary focusing usually changes the spacing between lens elements and the sensor, or moves internal elements, so the required image plane lands on the sensor. A simple fixed lens retains its focal length when the object moves. Some internal-focus designs do change effective focal length slightly, but that is a consequence of rearranging the optical system.
Then what does the number written as an f-stop compare? Is it measuring the clear hole, the focal length, or some combined amount that predicts both brightness and background blur?

An f-number is the focal length divided by the effective aperture diameter. A lower number means a wider relative opening, generally admitting more light and reducing depth of field for the same framing conditions. Because it is a ratio, the same physical hole can represent different f-numbers on lenses with different focal lengths.

Why does the sharp picture move when I move the object, even though the lens stays put? I thought each object distance gives the lens a different focal length, but diagrams keep marking one fixed focus point.

The fixed mark is the lens's focal point for parallel incoming rays. A nearer object sends more strongly spreading rays, which need a longer distance after the lens to converge. A farther object sends less spreading rays, so they meet closer to the focal plane. Thus image distance changes while the lens's focal length remains fixed.
Is there a simple connection between the two distances, or is the new picture position something found only by drawing lines? I want to know why a small move near the focus causes such a large shift.

For a thin lens, the relationship is one over focal length equals one over object distance plus one over image distance. When the object distance is only slightly greater than the focal length, their reciprocal values are nearly equal, leaving a very small reciprocal for image distance. A small object shift can therefore imply a very large image shift.
What happens at the other extreme when the object is very far away? Does the image squeeze right onto the focus mark, and would it then become too small to have any recognizable detail?

As object distance becomes very large, the image plane approaches one focal length behind the lens. The image can be small, but detail is not automatically lost: its size depends on the object's angular extent and the focal length. The Moon is distant yet forms a finite image because it spans a noticeable angle in the sky.

If I exchange the wall and the glowing object without moving the lens, should the light rebuild the object at its old place? That sounds plausible, but ordinary objects do not send light as tidy points.

In ideal optics, light paths are reversible. If a patterned light source is placed in the former image plane, the lens forms its image in the former object plane, with the distance roles exchanged. An ordinary illuminated object is also a collection of points sending many rays, so tidiness is not required; enough rays merely need to enter the lens.

How can two lenses make a much larger distant view when neither piece looks especially wide? I assumed magnification only depends on glass size, so a narrow telescope should not be able to enlarge much.

A telescope's angular magnification mainly comes from the ratio of the objective's focal length to the eyepiece's focal length, not their widths. The objective forms an intermediate image of the distant scene. The eyepiece then lets your eye inspect that image under a larger angle. Diameter chiefly affects brightness and fine-detail resolution.
What is the middle picture between the lenses? Is it a real tiny scene that I could catch on paper, or is it only another apparent view meant for the second lens?

In a common astronomical telescope, the objective forms a real, inverted intermediate image near its focal plane. You can remove the eyepiece and place a small screen there to catch it. The eyepiece is positioned so that this intermediate image lies near its own focal plane, producing a comfortable magnified virtual view.
Why does a longer front lens and a shorter eye lens give more enlargement? The words longer and shorter refer to distances, but the result I see is an angle, which feels unrelated.

The objective turns a small incoming angle into a physical height at its focal plane; a longer objective focal length makes that height larger. The eyepiece converts that height back into an outgoing angle; a shorter eyepiece focal length makes the angle larger. Combining both conversions gives approximately their focal-length ratio.
If I separate the lenses more, does the front lens gain focal length because its picture has farther to travel? I would expect that to increase the enlargement without changing either piece of glass.

Separating them does not change either lens's focal length. A correctly adjusted telescope places the objective's image near the eyepiece's focal plane. Changing separation shifts that image relative to the eyepiece, mainly altering focus and whether outgoing rays are comfortable for the eye. It does not provide the straightforward magnification increase you expect.
What does the width of the front lens improve if not enlargement? A larger opening looks as though it should at least reveal smaller features rather than merely making the same blurred view brighter.

It improves both light collection and diffraction-limited resolution. A wider objective gathers more light from faint objects and allows finer angular details to remain distinct. The eyepiece can enlarge whatever detail the objective captured, but it cannot recover detail that a small objective blurred together. Width therefore matters greatly, just not as the main magnification control.
If I cover the left half of a lens, why does the right half of the picture not vanish? I thought a lens worked like a window, with each glass area carrying the matching area of the view.

Each point on the object sends rays toward many parts of the lens. Either half therefore receives information from the whole object and can form the whole image. Covering the left half removes roughly half the rays contributing to every image point, so the picture becomes dimmer rather than losing its right or left side.
What if I leave only a tiny clear corner instead of a full half? Would the entire scene still appear, and would it be shifted because the remaining light comes through off to one side?

The entire scene can still appear if that corner receives rays from all its points. In an ideal thin lens, those rays still head toward the same image locations, so the image is not substantially shifted. It becomes much dimmer, and diffraction or off-axis imperfections may soften or distort it.
Surely using the full lens must make the picture larger, because the outer light reaches farther across the wall. Why else would magnification depend on lens size at all?

Magnification does not ordinarily depend on the clear diameter. Outer rays from one object point travel at steeper angles but still converge on that point's assigned image location; they do not extend the picture's boundary. Diameter changes brightness, diffraction, and aberrations. Focal length and the object-image distances set the image's overall size.
Why might the uncovered corner produce a slightly worse shape if the ideal meeting points are unchanged? Is that because real glass has uneven bending away from the middle?

Partly. Real lenses do not bring every ray to exactly the ideal point, especially far from the optical axis or near the outer edge. Using an off-center patch samples asymmetric aberrations such as coma and astigmatism. Manufacturing errors can contribute too, but even a perfectly made spherical lens has predictable off-axis imperfections.

If I slide that tiny opening across the covered lens, could I compare the little views to test different areas? I am unsure whether each view should brighten the same places or reveal different errors.

Yes. Moving a small aperture across the lens selects different ray bundles while preserving the whole scene. Differences in image position, sharpness, or distortion reveal local slope errors and systematic aberrations; brightness may also vary because of coatings or blockage. This idea underlies several optical tests, although precise measurements need controlled point sources and geometry.
Does the same whole-picture rule explain why squinting can sharpen a blurry view? My eyelids leave only a narrow opening, yet I do not see merely a thin stripe of the scene.

Yes. The narrower opening blocks many rays from every scene point rather than selecting one stripe of the scene. Smaller ray bundles make defocus circles on the retina smaller, so the view can seem sharper. It also reduces light and introduces diffraction if extremely narrow, which is why squinting is a limited optical workaround.
What is the curved glass actually doing that flat glass cannot do? I think the middle is thicker simply to delay those rays more, and a bigger lens should delay more and magnify more.

The crucial effect is direction change at surfaces where the refractive index changes. Curvature gives different surface tilts at different heights, so rays are redirected by different amounts toward a common point. Extra travel time through the thicker middle is related to the wave description, but diameter alone does not set magnification.
Why does light change direction at the surface in the first place? Saying it slows down in glass seems incomplete, because a car slowing on a road does not automatically turn toward the middle.

The turning occurs when one side of a wavefront enters the slower material before the other side. That side advances more slowly while the other continues faster, rotating the wavefront and therefore the travel direction. If the whole wave enters straight on at once, it slows without turning. This relationship is summarized by Snell's law.
Does the second surface undo the first bend when light leaves the glass? The outside air is the original material again, so I would expect the ray to return to its starting direction.

It would return to its original direction if the second surface were parallel to the first, as in a flat window pane. In a lens, the two surface normals generally point in different directions. The second refraction therefore does not simply undo the first; together the two bends produce convergence or divergence.
If I put the same lens under water, would its focus move because the object appears closer, or because the glass itself bends less strongly when water surrounds it?

The lens itself becomes optically weaker because water's refractive index is closer to that of glass than air's is. Each boundary causes less direction change, so a converging glass lens generally gets a longer focal length in water. Apparent object position can also matter in a mixed setup, but the surrounding medium directly changes lens power.
Why can one lens picture be caught on a card while another can only be seen by looking through the glass? I assume the card version happens when the lens is physically larger and throws more light.

Catchability depends on whether rays physically converge, not mainly on lens diameter. A real image forms where rays from each object point actually meet, so a card can intercept the pattern. A virtual image forms where spreading rays only appear to originate when traced backward; your eye can interpret those directions, but a card cannot collect an apparent crossing.
What does my eye add that the card lacks? Both receive light at their surfaces, so it sounds as though the eye is making a second picture from the directions rather than catching the first one.

Exactly. Your eye contains another converging lens that takes the incoming directions and forms a real image on the retina. The brain interprets those directions as coming from locations in the scene. A plain card only scatters whatever intensity pattern reaches its surface; it has no lens to reorganize a diverging bundle into focused retinal points.
If I add a second lens before the card, can it turn any virtual picture into a real one? I am vague about where that second lens would need to sit.

Often it can. The first lens supplies rays with a particular spread, and the second lens can bend them into converging bundles if its power and position are suitable. For the second lens, the virtual image from the first system acts as an object described by the incoming ray directions. The required placement follows the lens equation.
Does moving the original object change the first lens's focal length when the picture switches from card-catchable to only apparent? The switch seems too sharp to come from distance alone.

The focal length stays fixed. The switch occurs as the object crosses the focal plane. Just outside it, outgoing rays converge very far away and make a real image. At it, they are parallel. Just inside it, they diverge and define a virtual image. A continuous change in ray angle produces the apparently sharp category change.
What would I observe exactly at that crossing point if I moved the object slowly? Would the card image grow without limit and become too dim before it disappears?

As the object approaches the focal plane from outside, the real image moves farther away and its geometric magnification increases. On any fixed card it goes out of focus, and a card moved to follow it receives light spread over a growing area, so it becomes dim. At the focal plane, no finite card position captures a focused image.
Why do simple lenses put colored outlines around a sharp-looking object? I thought every color followed the same route and lens width only controlled how large the shared picture became.

Glass bends different wavelengths by slightly different amounts, a property called dispersion. Blue light usually experiences a higher refractive index than red light, so a simple lens gives them different focal lengths. A screen at one plane cannot focus all colors perfectly, producing colored fringes. Lens diameter affects their visibility but not ordinary magnification.
What does a different focal length for each color mean when there is only one piece of glass? Is the focus mark really a stack of nearby colored places rather than a single point?

Yes, for a simple real lens the marked focus is an approximation, often specified for one reference wavelength. Parallel red, green, and blue rays can meet at slightly different axial positions. Each color also changes image size slightly away from the center, so chromatic blur may appear both along the axis and toward image edges.
Can closing the opening remove the colored edges, or does that only hide ordinary fuzziness? A smaller hole seems as though it would force all colors down the same central route.

Closing the aperture can reduce the visible blur because narrower ray bundles make smaller out-of-focus spots, especially for axial color error. It does not make the refractive indices equal or truly merge the focal lengths. Some sideways color scaling can remain. Very small apertures also add diffraction and reduce brightness.
Why do two joined lenses help if each one splits the colors? I would expect their mistakes to add, unless one piece somehow bends red more and blue less in reverse order.

That reverse balancing is the idea. Designers pair glasses with different dispersion and give one element positive power and another negative power. Their overall bending can remain converging while their color-dependent differences partly cancel. An achromatic doublet commonly brings two wavelengths to the same focus, though residual color remains across the full spectrum.
If I move the object, do those colored focal lengths move with it? I still tend to think the focal length follows the picture position whenever the subject distance changes.

The lens retains its wavelength-dependent focal lengths when the object moves. What moves are the red, green, and blue image planes associated with the new object distance. Their separations may change in practical terms, but that follows the imaging equation for each fixed color-specific focal length, not a focal length that tracks the object.
What causes the plain white blur near the edge even when I use only one color of light? Is that a separate failure of the curved shape rather than the color problem?

Yes. With one wavelength, spherical aberration can make outer and inner rays focus at different distances, while coma and astigmatism affect off-axis points asymmetrically. These arise from lens geometry rather than dispersion. Changing surface shapes, combining elements, or restricting the aperture can reduce them, but each remedy involves tradeoffs.
How does the eye keep a nearby page and a distant sign clear at different times? I assumed the eye lens changes focal length simply because the object moved, like any lens responding to distance.

An ordinary rigid lens does not respond to object distance, but the eye actively changes its lens shape. Muscles alter the curvature, changing optical power and therefore focal length so the image remains on the fixed retina. This active process is accommodation; it is not the object directly changing a passive lens.
Why can the retina not move forward and backward instead, as a wall does behind a glass lens? It seems mechanically simpler than squeezing the clear part into a new curve.

The retina lines the inside of the eyeball and is connected to delicate tissue, blood vessels, and nerves, so translating it would be mechanically difficult. Changing lens curvature provides a compact way to adjust optical power while image distance stays nearly fixed. Some animals use different focusing mechanisms, including moving a lens, but human eyes mainly accommodate by reshaping it.
Does the dark opening in front decide how large the retinal picture is? Since it gets wider in dim light, I thought it also magnified objects to compensate for seeing less detail.

The pupil mainly controls how much light enters and how broad the ray bundles are. Widening it does not substantially magnify the retinal image; eye geometry and optical power set that scale. A larger pupil helps brightness but reduces depth of field and can expose more aberrations, which may actually reduce sharpness in dim conditions.
What exactly changes when someone needs a distance lens in front of the eye? Is that extra glass moving the focus point back onto the retina without making the viewed object much larger?

Yes. Corrective lenses alter the vergence, meaning the convergence or divergence, of light before it enters the eye. They compensate when the eye's relaxed optical power or length would place the image in front of or behind the retina. They can cause some size change, especially with strong prescriptions, but refocusing is their main purpose.
When an object moves farther from a converging lens, I know the real image approaches the focal region. How does that happen if the focal point itself is fixed by the lens?

The focal point stays fixed; it is the image distance that changes. Rays from a very distant object arrive nearly parallel and converge close to the focal plane. For a nearer object, the rays reach the lens with more divergence, so the lens needs a longer distance after refraction to bring them together.
How does the lens account for that extra divergence? In a ray diagram, the principal rays look like special paths, almost as though only those rays are being focused.

The principal rays are just convenient representatives. Every ray from one object point is refracted according to the local surface angle and refractive index. If the lens is ideal, all those outgoing rays meet at the same image point. The three standard rays let you locate that point without tracing the full bundle.
When the object is at twice the focal length, the image is the same size and inverted. Why does moving inward make the magnification grow while the image keeps flipping direction?

For an object outside the focal length, the rays truly cross, so the real image remains inverted. As the object approaches the focal point, the outgoing bundle converges more weakly and meets farther away. That larger image distance relative to object distance gives a larger magnitude of magnification; the negative sign records the inversion.
How should I picture the transition right at the focal distance? Does the image briefly sit at infinity, or is infinity only shorthand for rays that no longer intersect?

It is both a mathematical limit and a useful physical description. At exactly one focal length, an ideal thin lens sends rays from each object point out parallel, so no finite screen can catch a focused image. Saying the image is at infinity describes that collimated bundle rather than a literal surface located infinitely far away.
A lens has two refracting surfaces, but diagrams often replace both with one bend at the center line. How do the two surface refractions combine into a single focusing action?

At the first surface, a ray changes direction as it enters the glass; at the second, it changes again as it returns to air. The curvatures make those changes depend on ray height. In the thin-lens approximation, the separation between surfaces is neglected, so the two direction changes can be represented by one equivalent bend.
When a ray enters near the upper edge, the surface normal tilts more than near the axis. Is that larger incident angle what gives the edge a stronger focal power?

Broadly, yes: the changing normal across a curved surface gives different rays different deflections, steering them toward a common point. But edge rays do not simply receive a perfectly proportional increase. For a spherical lens they often cross at a slightly different location, producing spherical aberration beyond the paraxial approximation.
How does the second surface help instead of undoing the first bend? Since the ray goes from glass back into air, I would expect the refraction direction to reverse.

The ray does bend away from the normal when leaving glass, but the second surface's normal points in a different direction. For a biconvex lens, that geometry usually bends the ray farther toward the optical axis. Reversing the index step does not reverse the whole path unless the interface orientation is also reversed appropriately.
If the lens were immersed in water, when would those two bends become too weak to form a nearby image? The glass still has curvature, but its relative index is smaller.

It still forms an image as long as the glass and water have different refractive indices, but the focal length becomes longer. Focusing vanishes in the limit where their indices match, because neither interface changes the ray direction. If the surrounding medium had a higher index than the lens, the lens's converging or diverging role could even reverse.
How thick can the glass become before the single central bend stops being a reliable model? Is thickness judged against focal length, surface radius, or the object distance?

There is no universal cutoff, but thickness matters when the distance traveled inside the lens is no longer negligible for the required accuracy. Comparing center thickness with curvature radii and focal length is usually more relevant than comparing it with object distance. Then you use two refracting surfaces or principal planes instead of one lens plane.
With a magnifying glass, the object is inside the focal length and the image is called virtual. How does an image have a definite position if no rays actually meet there?

After the lens, rays from each object point diverge, but they do so as if they originated from a particular point behind the object. Extending those rays backward locates that point. Your eye receives the diverging bundle and interprets it using the same directional cues it normally uses for light from a real object.
When I move the magnifier closer to the object, the enlarged view sometimes seems smaller. Is the virtual image sliding toward the lens even though the angular magnification can still change?

Yes. Deep inside the focal length, bringing the object closer to the lens moves the virtual image closer and reduces its linear magnification. What your eye perceives also depends on angular size and viewing distance. A smaller virtual image can still subtend a useful angle if its apparent position and the lens position are close enough.
How does my eye focus on that backward extension? It sounds as though the lens creates an imaginary object that the eye then projects onto the retina as a real image.

That is nearly the right chain. The magnifier produces a diverging bundle with the same vergence as light from the virtual image location. The eye accommodates for that vergence and its own lens forms a real image on the retina. Nothing is projected backward; the virtual location summarizes the directions of the rays entering the eye.
When could a second lens turn that virtual image into something visible on a screen? Would the virtual image act as the second lens's object, or does its sign change again?

A second converging lens can redirect the bundle so it converges onto a screen. For that lens, the incoming rays determine whether its object is real or virtual: if they are diverging from a point on the incoming side, that point is a real object for it. The signs depend on the convention, but the ray geometry is unambiguous.
How is that different from placing a screen where the virtual image appears? The location seems geometrically specified, so I would expect some concentrated light there.

The apparent location lies on the backward extensions, not on the actual outgoing paths. A screen there intercepts light before or on the wrong side of the lens, where rays from each object point have not converged. A real image requires actual rays from each point to meet at corresponding points on the screen.
When the object reaches the focal point, does the virtual image switch sides discontinuously? The lens equation changes sign, but the ray bundle seems as though it should evolve smoothly.

The bundle evolves smoothly. Approaching the focal point from inside sends the virtual image farther away; at the focal point the rays are parallel; just outside, they converge to a very distant real image on the opposite side. The algebraic image distance passes through infinity, so the side change is not a finite jump.
For two lenses made from the same glass, how does stronger curvature shorten the focal length? I understand that steeper surfaces refract more, but not when that becomes a linear effect.

Stronger curvature means smaller radii, so the surface normals rotate more rapidly with distance from the axis. In the paraxial limit, the lensmaker relation makes optical power proportional to combinations of inverse radii, multiplied by the refractive-index contrast. The relationship is linear in power, not generally in focal length, because power equals one over focal length.
When both radii are halved for a symmetric biconvex lens, should I expect twice the focusing strength and therefore half the focal distance, assuming the lens stays thin?

Under the thin-lens and paraxial assumptions, yes. Halving both signed radii doubles each inverse-radius term, so the optical power doubles and the focal length halves. In a real lens, changing curvature while holding thickness negligible may be impossible, and stronger curvature also increases aberrations that the simple relation does not describe.
How does a plano-convex lens compare if its curved side has the same radius as either side of that symmetric lens? Does the flat face contribute zero refraction?

The flat face has zero surface power in the lensmaker formula because its radius is infinite, but a ray can still change direction there if it arrives obliquely. For near-axis collimated light, a plano-convex lens with one matching curved radius has about half the power of a symmetric biconvex lens whose two surfaces contribute equally.
When does the orientation of that plano-convex lens matter? Its focal length should be the same either way, yet one direction is said to focus more cleanly.

Its paraxial focal length is essentially unchanged when flipped, but spherical aberration changes. For collimated light focused to a point, placing the curved surface toward the collimated beam usually distributes refraction more favorably between the surfaces. The best orientation depends on the conjugate distances, not on a change in first-order optical power.
The thin-lens equation often uses positive and negative image distances. How does the sign encode the physical image without making the equation depend on which direction I draw the page?

A sign convention ties signs to light propagation and to whether rays actually converge or only appear to diverge from a point. Different conventions exist, so the page orientation is irrelevant as long as definitions remain consistent. A common real-is-positive convention assigns positive distance to real objects and images and negative distance to virtual ones.
When magnification is negative, I read that as an inverted image. Is that negative value a direction of magnification, or only bookkeeping inherited from the height coordinates?

It is bookkeeping with physical meaning. Transverse magnification is the signed ratio of image height to object height. A negative ratio says corresponding points lie on opposite sides of the optical axis, so the image is inverted in that transverse direction. The magnitude tells the size ratio; magnification itself is not a spatial direction.
How does the formula distinguish an upright virtual image from an upright real one? Positive magnification seems to describe both possibilities if another optical element flips the object first.

Magnification alone cannot classify the image as real or virtual. Its sign only compares orientation with the chosen object. You also need the image-distance sign or the actual ray vergence. In a multi-element system, an intermediate image may serve as an object for the next element, so orientation and reality must be tracked separately.
When I switch to the Cartesian convention, why do some familiar formulas acquire extra minus signs? The rays have not changed, so I assume the focal power is being relabeled.

Exactly: the optics is unchanged, while coordinate definitions change. In a Cartesian convention, distances measured along one axis direction are positive and those measured opposite are negative. The algebra must reflect those choices, including signed focal lengths and radii. Rather than transferring signs between formulas, derive or record one internally consistent set.
How can I check a result without relying on memorized signs? Is drawing whether the outgoing rays converge or diverge enough to recover the image type and orientation?

A quick ray sketch is an excellent check. Determine whether outgoing rays converge to a real image or require backward extensions for a virtual one, then compare an off-axis object's image point with the axis to determine orientation. The equation should agree. A limiting case, such as an object very far away, provides another reliable check.
Closing a camera aperture makes the image dimmer, which is clear, but how does it also make more distances look focused when the lens still has one image plane?

Only one object plane is exactly conjugate to the sensor plane. Points away from that plane form small blur disks instead of points. A smaller aperture narrows each cone of rays, so those disks become smaller at the fixed sensor. More object distances then fall below your chosen sharpness threshold, creating greater depth of field.
When the aperture becomes very small, could every object distance become exactly sharp because the ray cones approach single lines? Or is that only increasing the acceptable focus zone?

It only increases the range that appears acceptably sharp. Geometric blur shrinks, but exact image distances remain different for different object distances. Moreover, a very small aperture introduces diffraction: each point spreads into an Airy pattern. Eventually diffraction softening grows enough that stopping down further reduces overall detail rather than improving it.
How does the circle of confusion relate to the lens equation? I tend to think of it as the focal spot getting wider, although the ideal convergence point is elsewhere.

The lens equation gives the axial location where an ideal point's cone would converge. If the sensor sits before or after that location, it cuts the cone at a finite cross-section: the circle of confusion. Its diameter follows from similar triangles and depends on aperture diameter and the separation between the sensor and ideal image plane.
When does changing aperture move the actual focus? In the ideal model it should not, but real photographs sometimes show a small focus shift after stopping down.

An ideal thin lens has no aperture-dependent focal position. Real lenses with spherical aberration focus marginal and paraxial rays at slightly different distances. A wide aperture includes both; stopping down removes more marginal rays, shifting the location of best compromise focus. Lens design and focus breathing can complicate the observed shift further.
How is the depth of field split in front of and behind the focused distance? People say one third and two thirds, but that sounds like a fixed focusing ratio.

The one-third/two-thirds rule is only a rough special case. The distribution depends on focal length, aperture, focus distance, and the allowed circle of confusion. At close distances it is closer to symmetric around the focused plane; near the hyperfocal distance, the far region can extend to infinity while the near region remains finite.
When focusing at the hyperfocal distance, is infinity literally on the same image plane, or merely blurred by exactly the maximum circle that was declared acceptable?

Infinity is not exactly focused unless the lens is set to infinity. At the hyperfocal setting, the sensor lies slightly away from infinity's ideal focal plane, so distant points form circles of confusion at the selected acceptable limit. The usefulness of the setting therefore depends on viewing size, resolution, eyesight, and the chosen sharpness criterion.
White light passing through a simple lens forms colored fringes near focus. How does dispersion turn one focal point into several if every color crosses the same curved surfaces?

The surfaces are the same, but the glass's refractive index varies with wavelength. Shorter wavelengths usually experience a larger index and therefore greater optical power, reaching focus closer to a positive lens. Each spectral band has its own focal distance, producing longitudinal color blur and, away from the center, differently scaled images.
When the sensor is placed between the red and blue focal planes, why can a green edge appear beside a magenta one? I expected separate colored copies instead of paired borders.

A defocused wavelength spreads light across an edge rather than making a clearly separated copy. At a chosen sensor plane, some wavelengths may be tighter while others spill to opposite sides of high-contrast transitions. Their additive combinations can produce green on one side and magenta on the other, depending on focus position and lens correction.
How does an achromatic doublet bring two colors together? Is the diverging element adding negative dispersion while preserving most of the first lens's positive convergence?

That is the basic strategy. A positive low-dispersion crown element is paired with a negative higher-dispersion flint element. Their powers are chosen so the combined system remains converging while their wavelength-dependent power changes cancel at two selected wavelengths. Other wavelengths still have residual secondary spectrum, so the correction is not perfect.
When would lateral chromatic aberration remain even if axial colors share a focus? Does it come from wavelength-dependent magnification rather than a different focal surface?

Yes. Lateral chromatic aberration is mainly a wavelength-dependent image scale, so red, green, and blue versions of an off-axis point land at different transverse positions. It grows toward the field edges and is not removed simply by choosing another sensor plane. Correcting it requires controlling chromatic power across the whole optical system.
A spherical lens does not bring all parallel rays to exactly one point. How do marginal rays end up focusing sooner when the surface is supposed to have one constant curvature?

Constant curvature means the surface belongs to a sphere, not that every ray experiences an equivalent geometry. Farther from the axis, surface normals are tilted more strongly, and Snell's law produces deviations that depart from the paraxial linear relation. For a typical positive spherical lens, marginal rays therefore cross the axis closer to the lens.
When texts restrict rays to the paraxial region in practice, are they making Snell's law approximate, or only replacing the trigonometric angles with small-angle versions?

Snell's law itself remains exact. The paraxial treatment approximates sines and tangents by their angles and keeps only first-order terms in ray height and angle. Under those assumptions, refraction becomes linear and all rays from an object point share one Gaussian image point. Higher-order terms describe aberrations such as spherical aberration.
How does an aspheric surface correct the marginal focus? I picture its outer zones being flatter, but I am unsure whether that is always the required shape.

An asphere changes the normal directions zone by zone so marginal rays receive the deflection needed to meet the paraxial focus. For a given positive-lens task, that often means departing from the spherical profile in a way that reduces excessive edge bending, but the exact sag can be steeper or flatter depending on indices and conjugates.
When I stop the lens down, does spherical aberration disappear or just become hidden because the aperture rejects the rays with the wrong focal length?

It is mostly suppressed rather than corrected. The physical surface still gives different zones different focal behavior, but a smaller stop blocks the marginal zones that contribute the largest error. The remaining rays form a tighter spot, at the cost of light and eventually diffraction. Residual aberration can persist even within the reduced aperture.
How is the best focus chosen when the rays cross over a range of distances? Is it the smallest geometric disk, or does diffraction change where that focus plane belongs?

Geometrically, one common choice is the plane of least confusion, where the ray bundle has its smallest cross-section. For actual imaging, best focus depends on the metric: peak intensity, contrast at a chosen spatial frequency, or total wavefront error can select slightly different planes. Diffraction combines with aberration, so wave-optical optimization is more meaningful.
When two thin lenses are separated, how does the first image become the object for the second? I can combine their powers only when they are touching, so the gap seems optically active.

Trace the first lens independently to find where its rays would converge. At the second lens, those incoming rays may still be converging, already diverging, or exactly focused there. Their vergence defines the second lens's object distance. The air gap changes that vergence through propagation, which is why separated powers cannot simply be added.
How can the second lens have a virtual object if the first lens is forming a real image? Is that when the second lens intercepts the rays before their crossing point?

Exactly. If the second lens sits before the first lens's intended real image, its incoming rays are converging toward a point on its outgoing side. That point is a virtual object for the second lens. The label refers to where the rays are headed before refraction, not to whether the upstream lens was capable of forming a real image.
When does the pair become afocal? I know the separation is related to the two focal lengths, but I sometimes treat that as the lenses sharing one focus.

An afocal pair converts a parallel input bundle into a parallel output bundle. For two positive thin lenses, that occurs when their separation equals the sum of their focal lengths: the rear focal point of the first coincides with the front focal point of the second. They share a focal plane, not a single focal point belonging to both.
How does an afocal telescope enlarge an image if the final rays are still parallel? There is no final real image until the eye or another lens receives them.

It enlarges angularly rather than producing a larger final plane image by itself. The objective turns each distant field angle into a position at the shared focal plane. The eyepiece converts that position back into a different outgoing angle. Your eye then focuses the parallel bundle onto the retina, where the larger angle produces a larger retinal image.
When one lens in the pair is negative, why is the afocal spacing a difference rather than a sum? Does the virtual focal point count as a negative physical gap?

The focal lengths are signed, so the same algebraic condition can be written as a signed sum. A negative lens has a virtual focal point on the side from which collimated light arrives. The physical spacing stays positive; the negative focal length reduces the required distance because the relevant focal locations lie differently along the axis.
How would moving the lenses slightly away from the afocal spacing show up in the output? Would distant objects gain a finite image distance, or mainly look out of focus to the eye?

The output acquires nonzero vergence, so a collimated input no longer leaves collimated. It then has a finite real or virtual focus depending on the direction of the spacing error. An accommodating eye may compensate for a modest error, making the view seem focused but less comfortable; a camera fixed at infinity would record defocus.
The eye keeps the retinal distance nearly fixed, yet it focuses from distant objects to nearby ones. How does accommodation alter the lens equation without moving the image screen?

Accommodation changes the eye's optical power. The ciliary system allows the crystalline lens to become more curved for near objects, shortening its effective focal length so the image still lands on the retina. For distant objects, the lens is flatter and weaker. The retina stays fixed while the object distance and focal power trade off.
When the crystalline lens becomes rounder, is most of the added refraction at its front surface? I assume the cornea remains the stronger fixed focusing element.

The cornea supplies most of the eye's total static power because of the large air-to-cornea index change. Accommodation comes from shape changes in the crystalline lens, involving both surfaces and its internal gradient of refractive index. The front-surface curvature changes noticeably, but assigning all added power to one interface is too simple.
How does farsightedness interfere with that process? Is the relaxed focal point behind the retina, requiring accommodation to pull the image forward even for distant light?

In hyperopia, the eye is too weak or too short for its relaxed power, so parallel rays would focus behind the retina. A person with sufficient accommodation can add power and bring distant images forward onto the retina, then add still more for near objects. This extra demand can become difficult as accommodative range decreases.
When a positive corrective lens is added, how does it avoid forming an image before light reaches the eye? Is it creating a virtual object at the eye's far point?

For ordinary viewing, the positive spectacle or contact lens gives incoming rays some convergence but does not bring them to a focus before the eye. The eye receives a bundle equivalent to one from an object within its focusing range. Describing the correction through the eye's far point is especially useful for refractive errors and lens prescriptions.
A projector produces a real enlarged image on a screen. How does moving the projector lens a few millimeters bring a distant screen into focus when the object slide barely changes position?

The slide or imaging panel sits only slightly beyond the lens's focal plane. In that region, a small change in object-to-lens spacing causes a much larger change in image distance. Moving the lens changes both conjugate distances, allowing the real image plane to coincide with the screen while the projector body remains essentially fixed.
When the screen is moved farther away, does the projected image necessarily become larger? I think the magnification grows, but the lens may also need to move toward the slide.

For a fixed lens and slide, increasing the required image distance generally increases the magnitude of magnification. Refocusing requires the slide-to-lens distance to move closer to one focal length, so the lens usually shifts relative to the slide. Practical projectors may move internal groups, but the conjugate relation still produces a larger image at longer throw.
How does the screen receive every image point without also showing the crossing rays from neighboring points as a haze? Those rays occupy the same space near the lens.

Ray bundles from many object points overlap in space, but direction carries their information. The lens redirects each bundle so rays from one object point reconverge at one corresponding screen point. At the correct plane, neighboring bundles have different convergence centers. Scattering by the screen then sends light from each formed point toward many viewers.
When someone blocks half the projector lens, why does the whole image remain instead of losing half its field? I would expect each lens region to own a section of the picture.

Each small region of the lens receives rays from nearly every point on the slide, so it contributes to the whole image rather than one field section. Blocking half removes part of every point's ray bundle. The complete image remains but becomes dimmer, and its diffraction and aberration pattern may change slightly.
How does keystone distortion fit into lens image formation? The top and bottom are focused by the same lens, yet a tilted screen gives them different magnifications.

A tilted screen intersects the projected ray geometry at different distances across its height. The farther portion samples the expanding image bundle later and therefore at a larger scale than the nearer portion. It may also lie outside the best-focus plane. Keystone correction prewarps the source or shifts optical geometry; it is not ordinary uniform lens magnification.
In a camera, how does moving the sensor relative to the lens select one object distance? Light from all distances enters together, so I am unclear how one plane gets priority.

The lens creates a different ideal image distance for each object distance. Placing the sensor at one of those image planes makes rays from that object plane converge sharply on its surface. Rays from nearer or farther objects cross before or after the sensor, so the sensor intercepts them as blur disks rather than points.
When autofocus moves a lens group instead of the sensor, is it changing focal length or merely shifting the back focal plane? The two effects seem mixed in a compound lens.

In an ideal unit-focus lens, moving the whole lens changes its distance to the sensor without changing focal length. Internal-focus designs move selected groups, which changes the system's principal planes and often its effective focal length slightly. Thus the image plane is repositioned, but magnification and field of view can also change, producing focus breathing.
How does the sensor distinguish a slightly defocused point from a physically larger object detail? Both could cover several pixels with a similar intensity patch.

A single isolated patch may be ambiguous. Focus systems use broader evidence: phase-detection compares rays from different pupil regions to estimate the direction and amount of defocus, while contrast detection searches for the lens position that maximizes fine spatial contrast. Scene structure, multiple edges, and sometimes learned priors help separate blur from object size.
When phase detection says focus is in front or behind, how do two pupil samples encode that sign? Are they effectively viewing two shifted versions of the image?

Yes. Opposite parts of the pupil provide two sub-aperture views. If the sensor plane is displaced from the true image plane, the two views show corresponding features shifted relative to each other. The direction of that disparity indicates front or back focus, and its magnitude estimates how far the focusing group should move.
How does pixel size enter the acceptable focus calculation? A circle of confusion smaller than one pixel sounds invisible, but sampling and color filters may complicate that cutoff.

Pixel pitch sets one relevant scale, but not a hard visibility boundary. The optical point-spread function, antialiasing filter, color-filter mosaic, demosaicing, sharpening, and display enlargement all affect recorded detail. A blur diameter below one pixel can still reduce contrast near the sampling limit, while a larger blur may be unnoticed in a small output.
When the lens is focused beyond infinity, what image geometry is actually occurring? Infinity has no farther object distance, so the phrase seems to describe a sensor offset rather than a subject.

Correct. Focusing beyond infinity means the optical system is set so parallel incoming rays would come to focus on the wrong side of the sensor plane, usually because the lens is positioned slightly too close to the sensor. Lenses allow this extra travel to accommodate thermal expansion, wavelength shifts, manufacturing tolerances, and autofocus control margin.
An off-axis object point still forms an image point, but its rays are asymmetric through the lens. How does that asymmetry create coma instead of merely shifting the image sideways?

For an ideal paraxial lens, the asymmetry only maps field angle to image height. In a real system, different annular zones and azimuths of the pupil give slightly different transverse magnifications for an off-axis point. Their images do not coincide, producing a bright core with a one-sided tail resembling a comet.
When the aperture is narrowed, why does the comet tail shrink? Is coma another edge-ray focus error, or does the stop change which magnifications participate?

Both descriptions point to the same pupil dependence. Coma is a field-dependent aberration whose transverse error grows strongly with aperture. Stopping down removes outer pupil zones, reducing the spread of their differing image locations and therefore shortening the tail. The underlying lens remains comatic, and diffraction eventually limits further improvement.
How does field curvature differ from coma? I sometimes describe curved-field blur as the edge rays focusing closer, but that sounds similar to spherical aberration.

Field curvature concerns the best-focus surface across image height: even well-formed off-axis points may lie on a curved surface rather than a flat sensor. Spherical aberration concerns pupil zones for one object point, including on-axis points. Coma is an asymmetric pupil-dependent spread that grows off-axis. Calling all three edge-ray errors hides which edge is meant.
When a curved sensor matches that field in practice, would off-axis points become fully sharp, or would astigmatism still give separate tangential and sagittal focus shells?

A suitably curved sensor can remove defocus caused by the average field curvature, but it cannot automatically eliminate other aberrations. With astigmatism, tangential and sagittal ray fans focus on different surfaces, so no single sensor shape coincides perfectly with both. Optical correction is still needed to bring those surfaces together and control coma.
For a thick lens, focal length is measured from a principal plane rather than from the glass surface. How does an imaginary plane acquire a real role in forming the image?

A principal plane is an equivalent reference plane, not a physical refracting surface. The two real surfaces and the propagation between them transform paraxial rays in a way that can be represented by refraction at paired planes. Measuring object and image distances from those planes lets the familiar thin-lens equations reproduce the system's first-order behavior.
When can a principal plane lie outside the lens itself? That seems to place the effective bend in air, where the refractive index is not changing.

It can lie outside whenever the combined ray transformation requires that equivalent geometry. Strongly curved thick elements and separated compound groups commonly produce this. No bend actually occurs at the external plane; it is where extrapolated incoming and outgoing paraxial rays give the convenient unity-magnification mapping used to define conjugate distances.
How does the back focal length then differ from the effective focal length? I have treated both as the sensor distance for an object at infinity.

Effective focal length is measured from the rear principal plane to the rear focal point. Back focal length is measured from the last physical optical surface to that same focal point. They are equal only if the rear principal plane coincides with the last surface. Mechanical camera clearance depends on back focal length, while image scale depends on effective focal length.
When a telephoto design is physically shorter than its stated focal length, is that mainly because its rear principal plane has shifted forward beyond the lens barrel?

The key is that positive and negative groups shift the principal planes so the effective focal length exceeds the physical distance from the optics to the image. Depending on the design and reference direction, saying simply that one plane shifts forward can be ambiguous. The group combination, rather than a long empty propagation distance, supplies the required angular magnification.
How are principal planes found in practice? Could I trace one parallel ray and one central ray, or does a thick lens require a full matrix calculation?

In first-order optics, either method works. You can trace suitable paraxial rays through every surface, extend the input and output segments, and infer focal points and principal planes from their intersections. An ABCD ray-transfer matrix packages the same calculation more systematically and is especially convenient for many surfaces, spacings, and different surrounding media.

In the thin-lens model, is it best to interpret image formation as a mapping between conjugate planes, rather than saying rays literally converge to an image point? I am trying to separate the Gaussian approximation from the underlying wave-optical statement.

Yes. Conjugate-plane language states the geometric mapping cleanly: rays from one object point are redirected so that, within the paraxial approximation, they meet at one image point. Wave optics refines that point into a diffraction-limited point-spread function. The rays are useful trajectories of phase normals, not independent physical filaments carrying miniature pieces of the image.

Then the familiar construction using one parallel ray and one chief ray is evidentially sufficient only because the paraxial transfer is linear, correct? Outside that regime, two selected rays could intersect while the rest fail to share the same intercept.

Correct. For an ideal first-order system, the ray-transfer map is linear, so two nondegenerate rays determine the image location for that object point. With aberrations, their intersection is merely one sample of a distributed ray bundle. A meaningful image location then depends on a criterion such as centroid, least-confusion plane, peak irradiance, or best wavefront fit.

I said chief ray too loosely; I meant the ray through the optical center in the idealized diagram. For a real compound lens, does that construction have any invariant counterpart, or is it purely a thin-lens convenience?

It is mainly a thin-lens convenience. In a centered compound system, the useful invariant construction uses the nodal points: a ray aimed at the first nodal point emerges from the second at the same angle when object and image media have equal refractive index. Principal planes handle conjugate distances, while the actual chief ray is defined by the aperture stop.

So when teaching image reversal, would it be more accurate to attribute the inversion to the negative transverse magnification of the conjugate mapping, rather than to rays crossing at the focal plane? The latter sounds wrong for non-infinite object distance.

That is the more general account. Rays from different object heights exchange ordering as their bundles propagate through the system, producing negative transverse magnification at the conjugate image plane. They do not generally cross at the focal plane; that plane is the image conjugate only for an object at infinity. The crossing sketch is a consequence of the mapping, not its definition.

For a thick lens, how much physical meaning should I assign to the principal planes when explaining where the image forms? They can lie outside the glass, which makes an explanation based on refraction at a single effective plane potentially misleading.

Principal planes are bookkeeping surfaces derived from the first-order transfer matrix, not locations where all refraction physically occurs. They let a thick system obey the familiar conjugate equations when object and image distances are measured from the appropriate planes. Their position outside the glass is unproblematic, much as an equivalent lever arm can extend beyond a mechanism.

Does the separation between the two principal planes affect longitudinal magnification independently, or is it already absorbed into the front and rear conjugate distances? I am assuming the surrounding refractive indices may differ.

It is absorbed into the cardinal-point description once distances are referenced correctly. Longitudinal magnification follows from the conjugate relation and the transverse magnification, with refractive-index factors when the object and image spaces differ. The principal-plane separation matters when converting those reduced distances back to physical coordinates, but it is not an additional independent magnification parameter.

If the lens is immersed on only one side, the nodal points no longer coincide with the principal points. Is the angular relation through the nodal points still the cleanest way to describe apparent direction, or does reduced angle avoid confusion?

Reduced angle is usually cleaner. Across unequal media, the paraxial invariant is naturally expressed with n times the ray angle, and the nodal-point construction preserves actual angle only through its particular cardinal geometry. Using ray vectors such as height and reduced angle keeps the index change explicit and prevents accidental transfer of the equal-media rule.

Suppose the system is not afocal but its rear principal plane shifts as an internal group focuses. Can the sensor remain fixed while the effective focal length and object conjugate both change, or must one of those changes be constrained?

Both can change while the sensor remains fixed. Internal focusing moves group powers and separations, thereby shifting principal planes, effective focal length, and the object distance conjugate to the stationary sensor. The design constraints are imposed by desired focus range, aberration correction, and image scale, not by a rule that effective focal length remain constant.

Then manufacturer focal length markings during close focus describe the infinity configuration more reliably than the active first-order system. Is effective focal length at the focused configuration enough to predict field of view for a nearby planar object?

Not by itself.
